topic: An Introduction to Philosophy of Religion
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Pesach commemorates the Exodus from Egypt

options.text: The giving of the Torah at Sinai
The Exodus from Egyptian slavery — the angel of death 'passing over' Jewish homes marked with lamb's blood, the hasty departure (unleavened bread), the crossing of the Red Sea
The destruction of the Second Temple

items.reveal:
Pesach falls on 15 Nisan (March-April). It lasts 7 days in Israel (Reform Jews observe 7 days worldwide), 8 days in the Diaspora (Orthodox/Conservative).

The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night (and second night outside Israel). The Haggadah ('the telling') is the text recited — recounting the Exodus story through symbolic foods (matzah, maror, charoset), four cups of wine, and the four questions.

'Next year in Jerusalem' closes the Seder. The festival's themes of liberation have shaped social movements: the African American spiritual tradition (Go Down Moses), the Civil Rights movement (King invoked Exodus), liberation theology.
items.why: Judaism's major festivals carry specific historical content. Pesach is not generic 'spring festival' but a structured ritual recreation of a specific liberation narrative — central to Jewish identity for over two millennia.

items.title: Jihad means 'struggle' — and has a greater inner meaning
items.claim: What is the classical Islamic distinction between greater and lesser jihad?

options.text: Greater jihad is large-scale war; lesser jihad is small skirmishes

A widely cited hadith distinguishes the 'lesser jihad' (armed struggle in defence of the community) from the 'greater jihad' (the inner struggle against one's own ego) — though the hadith's authenticity is debated by some scholars
Jihad means only armed warfare; it has no inner meaning
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Scholars including Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and modern critics question the hadith's authenticity. But the inner-struggle understanding is found independently in Sufi traditions and in mainstream piety.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha are linked in Hindu cosmology
items.claim: How do samsara, karma and moksha relate?

options.text: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically by realising the unity of atman and Brahman
Karma punishes the wicked in this life only
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes towards death.
